analysis.one_liner: Keeps tax-credit apartment buildings affordable to low-income renters instead of letting owners convert them to market rate.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee until the 117th Congress ended, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Low-income housing tax credit apartments are meant to stay affordable for 30 years, but a loophole lets owners convert them to market rents after 15 years by selling to a buyer. This bill would close that loophole for buildings already in the program, keeping their rents restricted. It never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income renters in tax-credit apartment buildings built before 2019, whose homes would stay rent-restricted for the full 30-year commitment instead of possibly converting to market rates at year 15. Also, the public purse indirectly, since the tax credits were already spent to create these affordable units.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 'qualified contract' option that lets owners of low-income housing tax credit buildings convert to market rates after 15 years, for buildings that received their credit allocation before January 1, 2019 [S2][S3].
Under current law those buildings are subject to a 30-year affordability commitment, but the qualified contract option lets owners opt out and charge market rents at the 15-year mark [S2].

The bill requires that if such a building is sold, the price be set based on the rents the property can charge under the continued rent restrictions, so the sale does not trigger conversion to market rate [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners and investors in tax-credit apartment buildings who planned to sell after 15 years at a market-rate price, or to convert the units to market rents. Some economists would also note the rule could modestly reduce the resale value and thus the appeal of investing in tax-credit housing.

drawbacks.text: Owners and investors financed these buildings expecting the 15-year exit option; repealing it after the fact changes the deal for buildings already placed in service, and the bill would apply to written requests submitted after enactment [S3].
By lowering expected resale values, the change could make investors somewhat less willing to supply capital for future tax-credit housing, though the bill does not touch the credit itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward: the public already paid for these affordable units through tax credits, and the bill makes sure they stay affordable for the full promised period. The main cost falls on investors who counted on the early exit, and a fair-minded skeptic would note the possible chilling effect on future tax-credit investment, but the bill does not reduce the credit itself and applies only to existing buildings' exit rights.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Neguse introduced the bill on June 28, 2021 and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1][S5].
No other member cosponsored the bill [S4].
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote recorded before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners and investors in low-income housing tax credit buildings are better off, because they keep the option to convert their units to market rents after 15 years, and the tax-credit industry continues unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tax-credit property owners keep the exit option

for.name: Rep. Joe Neguse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it; no other member joined him.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat in committee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Did not schedule the bill for committee action at any point in the 117th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: With a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors, no vote or hearing ever revealed where either party stood.

industries.industry: Low-income housing tax credit property owners and investors
industries.note: These owners currently can sell tax-credit buildings after 15 years through a qualified contract and charge market rents; the bill would take that exit away and hold rents down for the full 30 years. Keeping the option lets them capture the full market value of property the public subsidized.

industries.industry: Tax-credit syndicators and affordable housing developers
industries.note: The bill leaves the low-income housing tax credit itself untouched, so the industry keeps its core subsidy; only the early-exit option disappears, which could slightly reduce resale values but also extends the stability of the housing stock the industry depends on.
